summary:
Civil Defense faces a major challenge in allocating limited resources as wildfire risk zones shift over time.

**Kepler** is an intelligent platform that recommends the optimal deployment of firefighting teams using an algorithm that analyzes historical fire patterns and harmonizes MODIS and VIIRS satellite sensor data from NASA FIRMS.

The project aims to enhance emergency preparedness, reduce response times and potential losses, and protect lives by transforming satellite data into informed, data-driven field decisions.
details:
Kepler: Intelligent Wildfire Monitoring and Firefighting Resource Allocation

Kepler is an intelligent wildfire monitoring and resource allocation platform designed to help emergency response teams make better decisions using historical satellite observations from NASA FIRMS.

The project addresses a critical challenge faced by civil defense authorities: allocating limited firefighting resources effectively as wildfire risk changes across different locations and over time.

How does it work?

Kepler transforms satellite observations into actionable information through three main stages:

  1. Satellite Monitoring: Uses NASA FIRMS data, incorporating MODIS (Terra and Aqua) and VIIRS (Suomi NPP and NOAA-20) satellite observations to identify potential wildfire hotspots.
  2. Data Analysis: Analyzes the geographical distribution and historical recurrence of fire detections to identify areas with repeated wildfire activity and higher risk.
  3. Resource Optimization: Simulates the strategic distribution of firefighting teams and proposes locations for fire stations and operational units based on historical hotspot concentrations and available resources.

The platform includes interactive maps, historical timelines, hotspot visualizations, and adjustable resource allocation simulations. We applied our model to Maui, Hawaii, using historical observations from 2000 to 2026, with particular attention to the 2023 Lahaina wildfire.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Kepler aims to improve emergency preparedness and support faster, more informed firefighting decisions. Its expected benefits include:

  • Improving the strategic allocation of limited firefighting resources.
  • Identifying areas with recurring wildfire activity.
  • Supporting proactive planning rather than relying exclusively on reactive responses.
  • Reducing potential response delays, property damage, and loss of life.
  • Helping civil defense authorities, municipalities, and local communities make data-driven decisions.

Our ultimate goal is to contribute to safer communities by turning satellite observations into decisions that can help save lives.

Tools, Technologies, and Data Sources

  • NASA FIRMS: Satellite-based fire detection data.
  • MODIS: Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer data from Terra and Aqua.
  • VIIRS: Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite data from Suomi NPP and NOAA-20.
  • Interactive geospatial maps and historical data visualization.
  • Web-based platform hosted through GitHub Pages.

Creativity and Innovation

What makes Kepler creative is its approach to transforming satellite fire detections into practical decisions about emergency resource allocation.

Instead of simply displaying where fires have occurred, Kepler examines historical patterns to identify recurring hotspots and simulates how firefighting teams could be distributed to improve preparedness.

It bridges the gap between Earth observation data and real-world emergency management, making complex satellite information more accessible and useful for decision-makers.

Factors Considered

During development, our team considered:

  • Historical wildfire frequency and geographical distribution.
  • Satellite detection data and differences between MODIS and VIIRS observations.
  • Thermal hotspot locations and Fire Radiative Power (FRP).
  • Spatial clustering and recurring hotspot concentrations.
  • The number of available firefighting teams and resource limitations.
  • Geographical coverage and the importance of strategic resource placement.

We also recognize that real-world deployment would require additional factors, including road networks, actual travel times, existing fire stations, available equipment, and weather conditions.

Future Development

Our next steps include expanding the model to additional geographical regions, integrating weather and wind data, and collaborating with firefighting authorities to improve the accuracy and practical application of our resource allocation recommendations.
